data.text/markdown:
Do Rossmann promotions change daily sales?

Research question: Do Rossmann stores have significantly different average daily sales on promotional days compared with non-promotional days?
  • Data: rossmann-store-sales/train.csv + rossmann-store-sales/store.csv (test.csv / sample_submission.csv ignored).
  • Design: observational — association only, not causal proof.
  • Primary test: Welch's t-test on log(Sales), two-sided, α = 0.05, H₀: μP − μN = 0 vs H₁: μP − μN ≠ 0.
  • Robustness: store-level paired t-test + Wilcoxon signed-rank.
Stage 1 · Load data

Dataset Shape Notes
train /rossmann-store-sales/train.csv 1,017,209 × 9 daily records, 1115 stores, 2013-01-01 → 2015-07-31
store /rossmann-store-sales/store.csv 1,115 × 10 store-level metadata

data.text/markdown:
Quality findings → cleaning decisions

  1. StateHoliday mixes bare 0 and the string "0" → normalized to string codes.
  2. 172,817 closed-store days (all Sales = 0, Customers = 0) are not trading days → excluded from the comparison.
  3. Open days with Sales ≤ 0 (rare refurbishment-like anomalies) → excluded and counted.
  4. No duplicated (Store, Date) keys; no missing values in train. store.csv structural missings (competition / Promo2 fields) are not used in the primary test.
  5. Promotions only run Monday–Friday (Sat share = 0.00, Sun share = 0.00) → promo status is confounded with day of week; the store-level paired design (Test B) partially mitigates store-level and weekday-mix differences.
No outlier trimming: high-sales days are genuine business volume.

Filtering audit trail
step rows removed rows remaining
start — 1,017,209
drop closed days (Open = 0) 172,817 844,392
drop open days with Sales ≤ 0 54 844,338
Final analytical sample: 844,338 open-store days across 1,115 stores, all with Sales > 0, so log(Sales) is defined.

data.text/markdown: EDA takeaway on confounders. Promo days concentrate on Monday–Thursday while closed Sundays pull down the non-promo mean; school-holiday incidence is similar in both groups (≈21% vs 18%), and state-holiday days are rare in either (~0.1%). Because promo status correlates with weekday and each store contributes many days, the pooled daily comparison (Test A) can overweight the promotion association. The store-level paired design (Test B) holds each store constant, giving a like-for-like estimate.

Stage 3 · Hypothesis testing

Two-sided, α = 0.05.
  • H₀: μP − μN = 0
  • H₁: μP − μN ≠ 0
where μP, μN are mean log daily sales on promotional / non-promotional days for open stores. We work on the log scale because raw Sales is right-skewed; effects are back-transformed to % uplift: 100 × (exp(mean log diff) − 1).

data.text/markdown: Stage 4 · Results and interpretation

Interpretation

Test A — Welch's t-test (unadjusted, pooled daily records). Mean sales are higher on promo days: €8,229 vs €5,930 (raw mean difference +38.8%). On the log scale the difference is 0.3462, i.e. ≈ +41.4% uplift (95% CI (41.1%, 41.6%)). n = 376,875 promo vs 467,463 non-promo open store-days. Welch t = 412.3, p = 0 — far below α = 0.05, so we reject H₀. Hedges' g = 0.89 on the log scale is not trivial, but note the imbalance: with 844,338 records even modest effects become detectable, so statistical significance alone is not evidence of commercial importance. Test B — Store-level paired comparison (1115 stores have both promo and non-promo observations; per-store promo-day counts range from 263–360). Within-store mean log difference = 0.3462, ≈ +41.4% (95% CI (40.3%, 42.5%)). Paired t = 88.8, p = 0; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 5.91e-184; Cohen's dz = 2.66. This is the more defensible estimate: it holds each store constant and compares like with like days within the same store. Statistical vs practical significance. The uplift is statistically detectable but its practical value depends on promo costs and margins, which we cannot see in this data. And because promotions are planned (weekday-only), stores differ in promo intensity, and other calendar effects remain uncontrolled, the association is not causal evidence.

Limitations and next steps

  • Observational data: promotions were chosen by store managers on weekdays; no randomization means we cannot read this difference as a causal effect.
  • Within-store dependence: ~943 store-days each; per-store clustering is only partially handled by the paired design — a mixed-effects or cluster-robust regression would tighten uncertainty bands further.
  • Weekday confounding: promos run Mon–Fri only, so Saturday and Sunday (usually stronger trading days) sit exclusively in the non-promo group. The paired estimate mitigates but cannot fully remove this.
  • Costs are invisible: higher revenue ≠ higher profit; promo cost data (discounts, lost margin) would be needed to judge profitability.
  • Heterogeneity: store type (a/b/c/d) and assortment may moderate the promo effect; a per-store-type breakdown is a natural extension.
Recommended next steps. (1) Quantify promo economics by combining this sales uplift with per-store promo cost data. (2) Examine heterogeneous effects across store types and weekends-opportunity stores. (3) Most decisively: run a randomized controlled promo experiment across similar stores to estimate the true incremental (causal) lift.
